Volume 09 · Chapter 11

Execution, trading costs and market microstructure

Advanced Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v09-c10

By the endEvaluate execution and liquidity effects on feasible investment strategies.

Turn a desired portfolio into a feasible sequence of trades

Capability. Evaluate execution and liquidity effects on feasible investment strategies. Specify order rights, measure signed trading costs, reconcile actual and paper wealth, and derive a constrained execution schedule before discussing capacity. The prerequisite is Alternative assets and illiquidity. We retain dated cash and portfolio conventions from Returns and payoffs, conditional information discipline from Market efficiency, anomalies and behavior, and the distinction between a chosen risk objective and a universal preference theorem from Mean-variance optimization.

A manager approves an investment at a midprice of 50. A trader reports buying at 49.90 and appears to have saved money. But perhaps this price was available only when the value subsequently fell, while the order remained unfilled when value rose. Or perhaps the trader bought only a small part of the approved position. Execution quality requires the original target, all order outcomes and a dated cash ledger. A favorable average price on selected fills is insufficient.

Every market, order, probability and coefficient below is an original synthetic teaching contract. There are no observed October 2026 prices or estimated commercial execution parameters. CU means currency units, prices are CU per share, quantities are whole shares unless a continuous relaxation is explicitly introduced, and interest is zero over these short case horizons. The cases are separate markets. A contract used in one case is not silently imported into another.

1. An order specifies rights, conditions and a deadline

A bid offers to buy; an ask offers to sell. A buyer demanding immediate liquidity normally interacts with available asks, and a seller with bids. The best quoted prices describe only their displayed quantities at their timestamps. The last transaction is a historical execution; the midpoint is a reference constructed from two quotes. Neither is a promise to transact the desired quantity. Quotes can change before an order arrives, and a large order can consume several price levels.

A market order prioritizes execution subject to the applicable trading contract. A buy limit places a maximum execution price; a sell limit places a minimum. A marketable limit may execute immediately. A nonmarketable limit may wait and never fill. Price protection is distinct from completion. An immediate-or-cancel instruction, abbreviated IOC here, cancels whatever cannot execute immediately. A fill-or-kill instruction, FOK, requires immediate full execution or cancellation of the entire order. A resting order has a separately specified lifetime and cancellation policy.

The SEC's March 2011 Trading Basics bulletin provides educational definitions of these order types and explains that broker offerings and policies vary. Its stop-order discussion distinguishes a trigger from a guaranteed execution price; a stop-limit also retains nonexecution risk. We use this dated terminology, not a statement about current venue rules or a universal default order lifetime.

For the first case, stipulate a single atomic snapshot: price priority, execution at each displayed resting price, no hidden liquidity, no new orders or cancellations during matching, and no routing elsewhere. Orders are independent alternatives against the same initial book. At a buy limit L only asks p ≤ L qualify; at a sell limit only bids p ≥ L qualify. Match the better prices first. IOC removes the residual after this one matching event. These assumptions make a transparent calculation; they do not describe every exchange, auction or broker.

Funding is also part of the instruction. This snapshot account has 100,000 CU cash and 600 existing shares. There is no borrowing or short selling. A buy must have cash for its fills plus fees, and a sell target cannot exceed its inventory. The examples have sufficient resources. More generally, a proposed order that violates these rights is infeasible even when enough displayed depth exists.

2. Measure spreads with a sign, a timestamp and a denominator

Let B and A be the best bid and ask immediately before arrival, with B < A. The quoted spread is A − B, and the arrival midpoint is m0 = (A + B)/2. Define the aggressor sign d = +1 for a buy and d = −1 for a sell. With execution price P and a specified later midpoint mh, define the following full-spread measures in CU per share:

Effective spread ES = 2d(P − m0).
Realized spread RSh = 2d(P − mh).
Signed midpoint component MCh = 2d(mh − m0).
ES = RSh + MCh.

The identity follows by adding and subtracting the same future midpoint. The factor two converts a one-way cost relative to the midpoint into a full-spread convention; it is not a second actual payment. Here basis points are 10,000 times each measure divided by the same arrival midpoint. Changing denominators or horizons can destroy a reported additive decomposition even when each input looks plausible. Fees are excluded from these price-spread measures and recorded separately in cash.

For an atomic order walking the book, we use its quantity-weighted execution price and the fixed midpoint just before that order's arrival. This is an aggregate arrival-reference measure. It need not equal an average of separately timestamped child-trade measures using changing internal quotes. For a sequence of orders over time, preserve each applicable quote and sign rather than manufacturing one convenient reference after observing the result.

The definitions and timestamp issues follow the measurement discussion in Hasbrouck's December 2025 teaching notes, sections 16.1–16.3. A later midpoint is a mark, not necessarily an available unwind. Thus realized spread is not automatically the counterparty's realized cash profit. The midpoint change can contain public news and other traders' actions; the accounting component alone does not identify the causal impact of this particular order.

Worked example 1 — Depth, cancellation and signed cost

The book is recorded at second 0, the alternative order arrives at second 1, and all snapshot fills occur at arrival. At second 11 the midpoint is 100.15. The one-way fee is 0.01 CU per executed share; cancelled shares pay no fee.

Independent initial snapshot; prices in CU per share
Bid priceBid sharesAsk priceAsk shares
99.90200100.10100
99.80200100.20150
99.60200100.40250

A market IOC buy of 300 fills 100 at 100.10, 150 at 100.20 and 50 at 100.40. Gross payment is 10,010 + 15,030 + 5,020 = 30,060; the average is 100.20. Fees are 3, so cash paid is 30,063. The top ask alone would understate the actual gross payment by 30 CU.

An IOC buy of 300 with limit 100.20 instead fills only 250. Gross payment is 25,040, average 100.16, and fees 2.50, for 25,042.50 cash paid. The other 50 shares are cancelled, not left resting. A FOK buy of 300 at the same limit fills zero, because only 250 shares satisfy the price condition. Its average execution price is undefined, represented by null in the lab. Treating that missing average as zero would manufacture spectacular price improvement.

The quoted spread is 0.20 = 20 basis points around midpoint 100. For the fully filled market order, ES = 2(100.20 − 100) = 0.40, RS = 2(100.20 − 100.15) = 0.10, and MC = 2(100.15 − 100) = 0.30. In basis points, 40 = 10 + 30. The spread exceeds the quoted spread because the order walks the book. These measures describe executed shares; they do not price the opportunity associated with the cancelled 50 shares in the alternative policy.

3. Why trade direction can convey information

Consider one share with eventual value V = m + δ or m − δ, each with prior probability one half, where m > δ > 0. Nature chooses V before an arriving trader acts. With probability θ, independent of V, the trader knows V and buys in the high state or sells in the low state. Otherwise the trader buys or sells with equal probability independently of V. The dealer observes only the direction, not the type. The uninformed order is an exogenous liquidity demand in this model; we are not deriving the customer's decision to participate.

The dealer is risk neutral, competition imposes zero conditional expected profit on each side, and there are no processing costs, inventory charges or tick restrictions. Quotes commit for one share and one arrival. They are updated before any later trade. We restrict 0 ≤ θ < 1 so that informed trading at the derived quotes is strictly profitable whenever informed traders occur.

Pr(buy) = ½θ + ½(1 − θ) = ½.
Pr(high and buy) = ½θ + ¼(1 − θ) = (1 + θ)/4.
Pr(high | buy) = (1 + θ)/2; Pr(high | sell) = (1 − θ)/2.
A = E[V | buy] = m + δθ; B = E[V | sell] = m − δθ.
A − B = 2δθ.

Bayes' rule supplies the conditional probabilities. A dealer selling at A receives A and delivers V, so zero conditional expected profit requires A = E[V | buy]. A dealer buying at B receives V and pays B, giving the analogous bid. A buy reveals more favorable information than a sell. It is therefore wrong to calculate both sides' expected profits using the unconditional value m after observing which side traded.

Informed traders earn δ(1 − θ) per trade, which the dealer loses. Against an uninformed arrival, the dealer's expected gain is δθ. Weighted across types these cancel: −θδ(1 − θ) + (1 − θ)δθ = 0. A positive spread can coexist with zero expected dealer profit. This supplies one mechanism, not a decomposition of any observed real spread. Inventory risk, processing expense, competition, discrete prices and the terms offered to customers require additional assumptions.

The same author's section 13.3 develops the conditional-order-flow mechanism. The symmetric parameterization, numbers and complete derivation here are our own. At θ = 0 this mechanism yields no spread; as θ approaches one, informed gains approach zero. At θ = 1 the prescribed informed trader is indifferent at the quotes, so participation needs an additional tie convention. The lab excludes that endpoint instead of silently assuming a trade.

4. A passive fill is a selected outcome

A limit order gives other traders an opportunity to transact with it under stated conditions. Being at a displayed price does not establish when its turn in the queue will arrive. Under a stipulated price-time queue with Q own shares, H shares ahead and S incoming eligible sell shares, the buy fill is min(Q,max(0,S − H)). Here S means volume that actually reaches this queue after better prices have been satisfied. Cancellations, hidden priority, new better orders and routing would change the calculation; they are excluded from this contract.

The queue and price process can be related. Orders may reach a passive bid especially when sellers are more willing to sell, including when value is falling. Conversely, an unfilled buy may miss a rise. Comparing the passive execution price only on filled orders conditions on a selected event. A meaningful policy comparison fixes the policy before those events and specifies what happens to the remaining quantity at the deadline.

Worked example 2 — Conditional information and deadline cash

First apply the one-trade information contract with m = 100, δ = 2 and θ = 2/5. A buy implies posterior high-state probability 7/10; a sell implies 3/10. Therefore A = 100.80, B = 99.20 and spread = 1.60. The dealer loses 1.20 per informed trade, weighted −0.48, and earns 0.80 on average per uninformed trade, weighted +0.48. The spread compensates for information selection under this contract.

Now use a separate passive-queue market; its probabilities are stipulated directly, not generated by the preceding dealer model. At the decision time, buy target Q = 100, midpoint = 50, immediate ask = 50.10, and fee = 0.01 per executed share for either passive or aggressive fills. Initial cash is 6,000. A passive buy at 49.90 has 80 shares ahead. There are no cancellations or new orders ahead. By the deadline exactly one row occurs:

Joint queue-volume and deadline-price scenarios, known only as a distribution at entry
StateProbabilityEligible sell shares SDeadline midpointDeadline askOwn passive fill
Fall2/518049.5049.60100
Rise3/58050.5050.600

The immediate policy buys all 100 now for 100(50.10 + 0.01) = 5,011. The passive-with-completion policy commits at entry to buy any unfilled shares at the stated deadline ask; sufficient depth at that ask is part of this separate contract. Fall costs 100(49.90 + 0.01) = 4,991. Rise costs 100(50.60 + 0.01) = 5,061. The 6,000 cash reserve funds both paths without borrowing. Expected completion cash is (2/5)4,991 + (3/5)5,061 = 5,033, which is 22 more than immediate execution.

Relative to a paper purchase at 50, immediate shortfall is 11. Passive completion shortfalls are −9 and 61, with expectation 33. To verify the wealth rather than just the price arithmetic, fall paper wealth is 6,000 − 5,000 + 100(49.50) = 5,950, versus actual 6,000 − 4,991 + 4,950 = 5,959. Rise paper wealth is 6,050, versus actual 5,989. The shortfalls are paper minus actual in each state.

Observed passive fills all occur at 49.90, followed by midpoint 49.50: their gross mark loss is 40 CU. The policy nevertheless outperforms the decision-price paper purchase in that falling state because it paid 0.10 less per share. The selected mark loss and implementation saving answer different questions.

An alternative policy cancels the residual at the deadline and never chases it. In rise it holds all 6,000 cash, so shortfall is the missed paper gain of 50, not zero. Expected shortfall is (2/5)(−9) + (3/5)50 = 26.40. This is 6.60 below mandatory completion because it avoids the rising-state deadline ask-minus-midpoint plus fee: (3/5)100(0.10 + 0.01). It also leaves the desired position absent in that state. It is a different mandate, not a free improvement to the complete-position policy.

5. Derive implementation shortfall from terminal wealth

Let Q > 0 be the original target quantity, d its buy/sell sign, pD the decision benchmark, pA the arrival benchmark, and pT a fixed terminal valuation price. Actual fills have quantities qj, prices pj and total f = Σqj ≤ Q; let F be total fees. The paper portfolio makes the entire signed trade dQ at pD. The actual portfolio makes only its fills and pays F. Both start with the same cash and inventory and are valued at the same pT. No interest, dividends or outside cash flows occur in this contract.

Paper gain from the target = dQ(pT − pD).
Actual gain from fills = dΣqj(pT − pj) − F.
IS = paper − actual = d[Σqj(pj − pD) + (Q − f)(pT − pD)] + F.

Expand the two gains and group the f executed shares and Q − f unexecuted shares to obtain the identity. Original inventory and unrelated cash cancel, which is why the same formula works for an investor selling existing holdings. A positive IS is a loss relative to the paper target; negative IS is a gain. An opportunity component is a counterfactual wealth difference, not an invoice. It can be negative when failing to transact happens to avoid an adverse price move.

One consistent decomposition assigns delay to the whole original target:

Delay D = dQ(pA − pD).
Execution E = dΣqj(pj − pA).
Opportunity O = d(Q − f)(pT − pA).
IS = D + E + O + F.

Substitution proves the equality: the arrival-price terms cancel. Another valid convention assigns delay only to f filled shares and measures the unfilled opportunity from pD. Combining full-target delay with opportunity from pD would count delay on the residual twice. State the convention before comparing desk reports. If no shares fill, the execution average is undefined but IS remains well defined. If all fill, opportunity is zero; delay can remain positive. Changing Q after seeing fills rewrites the counterfactual and conceals nonexecution.

Measurement also depends on the benchmark's purpose. An arrival price asks what happened after the order reached the trader or venue; a decision price includes the preceding delay. An external market VWAP is ΣviPi/Σvi for a declared universe of market trades and interval. It differs from the trader's own fill average. A TWAP averages representative prices using elapsed-time weights; equal weights apply only to equal-length intervals. Neither benchmark guarantees an executable quantity at its average.

Choose benchmark, timestamps, venue coverage, treatment of own trades and fees before seeing outcomes. Future market volume is unknown at the decision time. A schedule targeting an estimated volume profile can deviate from realized VWAP. An algorithm's name cannot remove price risk, market response or the consequences of noncompletion. Transaction-cost analysis also needs rejected, cancelled and unfilled orders, not just successful trade confirmations.

Worked example 3 — A small VWAP deviation hides a large target shortfall

At time 0, a cash-only account with 10,000 CU approves buying 500 shares at decision midpoint 20. At arrival time 1 the midpoint is 20.20. Fills are 200 at 20.25 at time 2 and 150 at 20.35 at time 3. The other 150 remain unfilled through valuation at time 4, when midpoint is 20.50. Fees are 0.02 per executed share, charged with each fill.

Gross paid is 200(20.25) + 150(20.35) = 7,102.50; fees are 7. Cash remaining is 2,890.50, and 350 shares are worth 7,175. Actual terminal wealth is 10,065.50. The paper portfolio holds 500 shares worth 10,250, so IS = 184.50 CU. Actual gain is 65.50 versus paper gain 250.

Decomposition gives D = 500(0.20) = 100; E = 200(0.05) + 150(0.15) = 32.50; O = 150(0.30) = 45; and F = 7. The sum is 184.50. Relative to target decision notional 500×20 = 10,000, this is also numerically 184.50 basis points. The numerical coincidence between CU and basis points comes from that particular notional, not a general conversion.

For a separate execution-only comparison, stipulate external market trades within times 1–3, excluding our fills: 1,000 at 20.10, 2,000 at 20.30 and 2,000 at 20.40. Market VWAP is 20.30. Our fill average is 7,102.50/350 = 2841/140 ≈ 20.292857. We beat market VWAP on filled shares by 2.50 CU before fees; after fees this comparison is a cost of 4.50. Neither number includes the decision-to-arrival move on the original target or its nonexecution opportunity. A good fill-relative statistic need not imply a good total implementation result.

6. Execution speed changes both expected cost and risk

The next model specifies a required monotone buy Q over two fixed-length blocks. Choose q1 at date 0 before observing a random shock ε. Buy q2 = Q − q1 at date 1 after that shock. The second quantity is the committed remainder, not a hindsight reoptimization that changes the target. Initially the unaffected midpoint is m. The shock is equally likely +s or −s, independently of our trade; E[ε] = 0 and Var(ε) = s² = σ². We require m > s so both unaffected prices stay positive.

Persistent impact increases the midpoint by k times cumulative shares bought, with k ≥ 0. It persists across these two blocks; nothing here asserts that our purchase changes eventual dividends or value forever. Within each block, the execution's persistent component is the average along the cumulative-quantity path. Temporary price impact is ηiqi for block i, where ηi > 0, and disappears before the next block. The fixed one-way half-spread plus fee is h ≥ 0. These supplied coefficients describe only monotone buys in this finite contract.

For a block starting at cumulative quantity z, averaging kx over x from z to z + q gives kz + kq/2. Therefore the first block's average all-in price is P1 = m + kq1/2 + η1q1 + h. Immediately afterward the midpoint, excluding temporary impact, is m + kq1. Then ε arrives. The second block starts at m + ε + kq1 and has average all-in price P2 = m + ε + kq1 + kq2/2 + η2q2 + h.

C = q1P1 + q2P2 − Qm
= kQ²/2 + hQ + η1q1² + η2q2² + q2ε.
E[C] = kQ²/2 + hQ + η1q1² + η2q2².
Var(C) = σ²q2².

The persistent term is ∫0Qkx dx = kQ²/2, equivalently k(q1²/2 + q1q2 + q2²/2). Multiplying the final displacement kQ by all Q would double this integral. The final marked inventory is not an additional purchase expense. Since h already contains fees, adding another fee line would also double-count. The cost benchmark remains the original unaffected midpoint m.

Define the decision score explicitly as J = E[C] + λ Var(C), λ ≥ 0. There is no factor of one half in this chapter's convention. C and J are CU, variance is CU², and λ is inverse CU. The coefficients k and η are CU per share squared; h and s are CU per share. This is a chosen mean-variance execution objective. With the binary shock it is not automatically identical to maximizing expected utility for an arbitrary investor, and it does not constrain a tail loss unless an additional restriction is imposed.

The cost-versus-risk formulation has primary research context in Almgren and Chriss's December 2000 manuscript, sections 1–2.1. Our within-block averaging convention, two-point shock, integer capacities and numerical cases are independently specified. Their discrete price convention includes a different temporary-coefficient adjustment; importing it into the prices above would be inconsistent. The lab implements the derivation here, not a reproduction of the paper.

Substituting q2 = Q − q1, the variable part is η1q1² + (η2 + λσ²)(Q − q1)². Its derivative is 2η1q1 − 2(η2 + λσ²)(Q − q1), with strictly positive second derivative 2(η1 + η2 + λσ²). Hence the unique unrestricted continuous solution is:

q1* = Q(η2 + λσ²)/(η1 + η2 + λσ²).

If capacities are u1 and u2, full completion requires max(0,Q − u2) ≤ q1 ≤ min(Q,u1). An empty interval means that the mandate cannot be completed within the contract. For a nonempty interval, strict convexity makes the continuous constrained optimum its projection onto that interval. With integer shares, compare the feasible floor and ceiling of the projected point; monotonicity on either side of the minimum excludes more distant integers. Ties can remain. Our lab reports all ties and selects the smaller first block.

When λ or σ² rises, the unrestricted first block weakly increases; differentiating with respect to λ gives Qη1σ²/(η1 + η2 + λσ²)² ≥ 0. Earlier trading removes exposure of the unpurchased remainder to ε but can use a more expensive block. With λ = 0 or σ = 0, this risk incentive disappears. Persistent k and fixed h do not change optimal timing for a fixed Q in this particular model because they contribute constants. They still affect total cost and optimal scale. Nonlinear or decaying impact, variable horizons, new signals or a sell program need a newly specified model.

Worked example 4 — Constrained timing and conditional capacity

Take Q = 12, m = 50, s = 0.5, k = 0.05, η1 = 0.2, η2 = 0.1, h = 0.1, and λ = 0.4. Block capacities are (5,9). The account has 1,000 CU, enough for every allowed schedule and shock in this example. The continuous unrestricted solution is 12(0.1 + 0.4×0.25)/(0.2 + 0.1 + 0.4×0.25) = 6. The feasible first-block interval is [3,5], so the constrained optimum is (5,7).

For (5,7), expected cost is 0.05×12²/2 + 0.1×12 + 0.2×5² + 0.1×7² = 3.6 + 1.2 + 5 + 4.9 = 14.70. Variance is 7²×0.25 = 12.25. Thus J = 14.70 + 0.4×12.25 = 19.60. Expected-cost minimization alone selects (4,8); the chosen risk penalty makes paying 0.30 more in expectation worthwhile to reduce variance by 3.75.

Actual average prices are P1 = 51.225 and P2 = 51.225 + ε. Initial payment is 5×51.225 = 256.125. The two possible deadline payments are 7×50.725 = 355.075 and 7×51.725 = 362.075. Total cash is 611.20 or 618.20, leaving 388.80 or 381.80. Relative to 12×50 = 600, realized costs are 11.20 and 18.20; their mean and variance independently recover 14.70 and 12.25.

If the first cap were relaxed enough, (6,6) would give expected cost 15.60, variance 9 and score 19.20. The cap raises the optimized score by 0.40 even though the constrained policy's expected cost is lower. An instruction to buy 15 with the original caps is infeasible because 15 > 5 + 9. It is not made feasible by quoting a very high cost or silently reducing the target.

Now suppose the investment committee separately authorizes quantity choice. Its supplied gross benefit is bQ with b = 1.50 CU per share, measured before execution costs and excluding any apparent gain from marking our own induced price movement. This is a planning benefit assumption, not estimated alpha. The authorized score is bQ − min J(Q), for integer Q from 0 through 14, including abstention. Optimize timing afresh at each quantity:

The score-maximizing size is 6, the largest size with nonnegative score is 11, and physical capacity is 14. They answer different questions. Several smaller odd-Q timing choices tie; the table uses the stated smaller-first-block rule. A mandatory Q = 12 remains a 12-share execution problem unless the committee changes it. None of these quantities is a general market-capacity estimate: benefits, uncertainty, impact, funding and allowable deadlines all matter.

7. Estimate an execution model without confusing a correlation with a mechanism

The finite optimizer is exact conditional on its inputs. Estimating those inputs is a separate task. Larger orders may be submitted precisely when urgency, information and expected volatility are higher. A regression of later price changes on trade size then mixes the order's own effect with selection and common news. Controlling for a future variable affected by the trade can create another bias. A causal impact claim needs an identification argument, such as a defensible exogenous change in routing or randomized scheduling within authorized risk limits, not just a positive slope.

Use consistent timestamps for decision, release to the desk, venue arrival, acknowledgments, fills, cancellations and valuation. Preserve rejected and unmatched orders. Synchronize quote and trade records; label missing or stale quotes rather than treating them as prices. Record size, spread, volatility, competing volume, queue state when available, and all explicit costs on the same currency and side basis. The future mark horizon and benchmark definition must remain fixed across comparisons.

A useful model evaluation compares later realized cost distributions with the forecast, including errors by order size and market condition. Report uncertainty in η, k, probabilities and benefit b, and rerun the decision under plausible alternatives. Capacity can fall because liquidity deteriorates, fees rise, the deadline shortens or a forecast weakens. A single linear fit outside its observed scale has no contractual force. Discretionary sizing also belongs to the mandate owner; a trader cannot improve apparent quality by dropping difficult portions of a required hedge.

The next investment-policy integration chapter connects approved targets, actual positions, cash, risk budgets and escalation. Execution reporting should retain all of them. The midpoint portfolio is a useful measurement counterfactual, while the investable portfolio is the one actually funded and filled.

Reproduce and challenge the finite contracts

Download the original input contracts, standard-library program, complete exact output, four-file integrity manifest and instructions and input domains. Rational results are exact strings, with null for an unobserved fill average. No network access or external package is needed. Reconstruct one order's cash, both passive scenarios, the paper-minus-actual ledger, and the two shock-state costs before using the optimizer.

The program checks convention labels as well as numerical domains. It rejects overfilled targets, trades before arrival, insufficient prefunding, unsupported priority claims, crossed snapshot books and the dealer's unspecified θ = 1 participation boundary. A required impact quantity beyond physical depth instead returns an explicit infeasible result; its independent authorized-size grid remains available. Run a zero-risk-penalty intervention, a queue-ahead intervention and the changed-benefit exercise below. An internally valid intervention is still a new conditional case, not evidence about a real venue.

Exercises

  1. Sell signs and a later mark. A seller-initiated trade executes at 49.95 against arrival midpoint 50; the specified later midpoint is 49.80. Compute ES, RS and MC in CU per share and basis points using the arrival denominator. Verify the identity and explain both a negative realized spread and the limits of calling MC causal impact.
  2. Inventory and executable depth. Against the unchanged independent snapshot in Worked example 1, sell 450 existing shares. Compare a market IOC, a sell IOC with minimum price 99.80, and a FOK sell with that same minimum. Give all fills, cancelled quantities, gross proceeds, fees at 0.01 per filled share, net cash and defined average prices. Identify the information needed before using this calculation for a real order.
  3. A new information spread. Use the one-arrival dealer model with values 96 and 104 and informed probability 1/4. Derive the direction-conditioned probabilities, quotes and spread, informed trader gain, dealer gain per uninformed arrival, and weighted dealer profit. Explain what θ = 0 implies and why θ = 1 needs a participation convention.
  4. Queue position and probability sensitivity. First change only the passive case's shares ahead from 80 to 100. Compute fills, remaining deadline buys, each path's total completion cash and expected completion shortfall. Compare with the immediate policy. Then restore 80 ahead and find the falling-state probability at which passive completion and immediate purchase have equal expected cost; the two possible volumes and quotes stay unchanged.
  5. A sell shortfall ledger. Start with 400 shares and zero cash. At decision time 0 approve selling all 400 at price 30. Arrival time 1 price is 29.90; sell 250 at 29.85 at time 2; terminal time 3 price is 29.70. The fee is 0.02 per filled share and there are no other cash flows. Derive paper and actual terminal wealth, full-target delay, execution, opportunity, fees, total IS and target-notional basis points. Explain why replacing the target by 250 is a change in the measurement question.
  6. Choose an honest benchmark. Independently calculate the external VWAP, own fill average, signed filled-only cost before and after fees, and full IS for Worked example 3. A report calls the 2.50-CU favorable gross VWAP deviation proof of execution skill and omits the unfilled shares. Provide a corrected report and an evaluation design. Explicitly identify which prices and quantities could not have been known at decision time.
  7. Risk preference, integers and binding caps. Keep the 12-share impact case and original capacities. Find the optimal integer schedule for λ = 0. Derive the nonnegative λ at which (4,8) and (5,7) tie, and show why (3,9) cannot improve on them. Separately find where the unrestricted continuous optimum first reaches q1 = 5. Explain why this second threshold differs from the integer switching threshold.
  8. Authorized scale is not an execution shortcut. Change only b to 2 CU per share in the separately authorized capacity decision; keep λ = 0.4 and all execution inputs. Use the complete cost grid to find the score-maximizing quantity, largest nonnegative-score quantity and physical capacity. Give the optimal schedule and score. A trader then proposes filling only that quantity on an unchanged compulsory order for 12. Evaluate the proposal, state who must authorize a target change, and give two specific model uncertainties that could change the scale decision.
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria

  1. d = −1, so ES = −2(49.95 − 50) = 0.10, RS = −2(49.95 − 49.80) = −0.30, and MC = −2(49.80 − 50) = 0.40. Dividing each by 50 and multiplying by 10,000 gives 20, −60 and 80 basis points; 20 = −60 + 80. The aggressor sold above the later midpoint. A counterparty that bought at 49.95 has a negative later mark relative to 49.80; that mark is not necessarily its actual unwind proceeds. News and other orders can drive MC. Correct evaluation requires all three signs, the common denominator, the specified horizon and the distinction between a descriptive mark and a causal estimate.

  2. The market IOC sells 200 at 99.90, 200 at 99.80 and 50 at 99.60. Gross proceeds are 19,980 + 19,960 + 4,980 = 44,920, average 4492/45 ≈ 99.822222, fees 4.50, and net cash 44,915.50. Nothing is cancelled. The limit IOC sells only 400: gross 39,940, average 99.85, fees 4, net cash 39,936, and 50 cancelled. The FOK fills zero because qualifying depth is only 400; all 450 are cancelled, gross and fees are zero, and the average is undefined.

    The initial 600-share inventory covers the target in each independent alternative. A real implementation also needs the executable book at arrival, queue/routing and priority rules, hidden or changing liquidity, fees and available inventory. The stipulated snapshot does not estimate their persistence during transmission. Answers must not rest the IOC residual or charge a fill fee to the cancelled FOK.

  3. m = 100 and δ = 4. Buy and sell probabilities are each 1/2. The joint high-and-buy probability is (1 + 1/4)/4 = 5/16, so Pr(high|buy) = 5/8; Pr(high|sell) = 3/8. Thus A = (5/8)104 + (3/8)96 = 101, B = 99, and spread = 2. Informed profit per trade is 4(3/4) = 3, and dealer gain per uninformed arrival is 4(1/4) = 1. Weighted dealer components are −3/4 and +3/4, summing to zero.

    At θ = 0, this mechanism gives both quotes 100 and zero spread because direction conveys no value information. It does not eliminate other omitted spread sources. At θ = 1, quotes would reach 104 and 96, making the informed trader indifferent between trading and abstaining. Without specifying participation, the assumed direction probabilities at this endpoint are not established. The lab's θ < 1 restriction is economically meaningful.

  4. With 100 ahead, fall fills min(100,180 − 100) = 80 passively and buys 20 at the deadline. Total cash is 80(49.90) + 20(49.60) + 100(0.01) = 4,985. Rise fills zero passively and buys 100 at 50.60; cash remains 5,061. Expected cash is (2/5)4,985 + (3/5)5,061 = 5,030.60. Expected shortfall is 30.60, still 19.60 more than the immediate policy's 11. Extra queue delay happens to improve fall's completion price because the deadline ask is below the passive price; it supplies no general ranking of queue positions.

    Restore 80 ahead. With fall probability p, passive completion cash is p(4,991) + (1 − p)5,061 = 5,061 − 70p. Equality with 5,011 requires p = 5/7. Passive has lower expected cost for p > 5/7 and higher for p < 5/7 within this unchanged contract. The calculation changes the probability of the complete joint scenario, not the fill probability independently of its accompanying price.

  5. The paper sale yields 12,000 cash. Actual sale proceeds are 250(29.85) = 7,462.50; after 5 fees cash is 7,457.50. The remaining 150 shares are worth 4,455. Actual terminal wealth is therefore 11,912.50, and shortfall is 87.50.

    Using d = −1, D = −400(29.90 − 30) = 40, E = −250(29.85 − 29.90) = 12.50, O = −150(29.70 − 29.90) = 30, and F = 5. Their sum is 87.50. In basis points it is 10,000(87.50)/12,000 = 875/12 ≈ 72.9167. Replacing Q by 250 would assess only a smaller intended sale and drop the original residual exposure; its shortfall would be 250(30 − 29.85) + 5 = 42.50. That different result is not a correction to the 400-share mandate.

  6. External traded value is 1,000(20.10) + 2,000(20.30) + 2,000(20.40) = 101,500 over 5,000 shares, so VWAP is 20.30. Own average is 2841/140. Signed filled-only VWAP cost is 7,102.50 − 350(20.30) = −2.50, or +4.50 after fees. Full-target shortfall remains 184.50, independently reconciled to terminal wealth.

    A corrected report supplies the original 500 target, 350 fills, 150 residual, all decision/arrival/fill/valuation timestamps, 7 fees and the chosen 100 + 32.50 + 45 + 7 decomposition. It presents the VWAP comparison as a different, filled-only benchmark. Future market trades, their volumes, the eventual fills and the terminal price were unknown at decision time; the benchmark rule and intended target could have been fixed then.

    For an evaluation design, freeze eligible orders and benchmark definitions, retain cancellations and failures, compare later costs and uncertainty conditional on mandate difficulty, and investigate selection or defensible randomized alternatives before attributing differences to skill. Grade correct arithmetic, complete-target reporting, information timing and an inference design separately. One realized favorable gross deviation does not establish repeated skill, causal impact or an optimal policy.

  7. With λ = 0, compare expected costs 14.70, 14.40 and 14.70: choose (4,8). The difference J(5,7) − J(4,8) is 0.30 + λ(12.25 − 16) = 0.30 − 3.75λ. Equality occurs at λ = 0.08 = 2/25 inverse CU. Below this choose (4,8); above it choose (5,7); at equality both minimize, and the lab's smaller-first-block rule selects (4,8). Also J(3,9) − J(4,8) = 0.30 + 4.25λ > 0 for every λ ≥ 0, excluding (3,9).

    The unrestricted continuous solution reaches 5 when 12(0.1 + 0.25λ)/(0.3 + 0.25λ) = 5. Thus 1.2 + 3λ = 1.5 + 1.25λ and λ = 6/35 ≈ 0.171429. The integer decision switches earlier, when the unconstrained minimizer crosses the midpoint 4.5 between integers 4 and 5. Reaching the cap continuously and preferring the integer at the cap are different events. Both results follow from the same strictly convex objective.

  8. For b = 2, the net scores for Q = 0 through 14 are 0, 1.675, 3.30, 4.475, 5.60, 6.275, 6.90, 7.075, 7.20, 6.875, 6.50, 5.675, 4.40, 2.675, 0.50. The maximum is 7.20 CU at Q = 8, with timing (4,4) and J = 8.80. The largest nonnegative-score quantity is 14, also physical capacity; the equality of those two quantities is incidental to these parameters.

    A compulsory 12-share order still requires its 12 shares and optimizes at (5,7). Filling only eight leaves four shares of unintended exposure. The mandate owner or designated investment committee must authorize the target change; the execution desk must report and escalate a mismatch rather than erase it. Uncertainty about benefit b, temporary impact, shock variance, available block depth or the cash requirement can change the scale decision. A strong answer identifies two specific changes and their route into benefits, cost, risk or feasibility, while distinguishing the supplied conditional calculation from an estimated real trading opportunity.

Teach-back and delayed retention

Teach-back. Explain to a committee why quoted spread, realized spread, whole-target shortfall and capacity are four different measurements. Benchmark answer: quoted spread concerns a timestamped top-of-book price pair and depth; realized spread uses a later mark and is not necessarily cash profit; shortfall compares the original paper target with actual funded positions including misses and fees; capacity requires both physical trading rights and an authorized benefit/risk objective. Demonstrate one cash reconciliation and identify who may change the target. Do not claim that an optimized conditional schedule authenticates its inputs.

Delayed check. First change only Worked example 1's later midpoint to 100.30. Answer: ES stays 0.40, RS becomes −0.20, and MC becomes 0.60; the arrival-reference identity still holds. Separately, complete the final 150 shares in Worked example 3 at time 4 for 20.60 with the same 0.02 fee, retaining terminal midpoint 20.50. Answer: total cash paid becomes 10,202.50, and full-target shortfall becomes 202.50 = 100 delay + 92.50 execution + 0 opportunity + 10 fees. The original 10,000-CU cash-only account cannot fund that completion: it needs 202.50 additional CU at or before the final fill. With an authorized extra 202.50 supplied equally to the paper and actual portfolios, their terminal wealth difference is still 202.50; without that funding, the proposed completion is infeasible. Relative to leaving the shares unfilled, the extra shortfall is 150(20.60 − 20.50) + 3 = 18.

Scope and deeper study

The chapter supplies exact snapshot matching, a one-arrival information mechanism, a correlated passive queue, a whole-target wealth identity and one constrained impact optimizer. It does not model every venue, prove that a particular broker achieves best execution, infer real impact coefficients, or identify a market's permanent causal response. Hidden orders, multi-venue routing, continuous-time stochastic control, dynamic learning, transient impact and empirically credible transaction-cost estimation are extensions requiring additional theory, data and institutional contracts.

The scoped source routes are SEC educational order terminology, Hasbrouck's conditional-information and measurement teaching sections, and Almgren–Chriss on execution cost and risk. Only the recorded sections were used for those methodological references. All numerical examples, exercises, queue scenarios and capacity decisions are original and conditional. The supplied code verifies the arithmetic and input contract; independent economic judgment is still needed to decide which model an actual mandate warrants.

Sources and further study

  • U.S. SEC Office of Investor Education and Advocacy — Trading Basics (March 2011) — Dated educational terminology for market, limit, stop, stop-limit, IOC and FOK instructions; distinction between price protection and execution; availability and broker-policy qualifications. The chapter's matching engine is an explicitly supplied original contract.
  • Joel Hasbrouck — Securities Trading: Principles and Procedures, version14c (13 December 2025), selected sections — Author-hosted primary teaching reference for order-direction conditioning and competitive quotes, and for execution benchmark, effective/realized spread and paper-versus-actual measurement distinctions. All chapter fixtures and derivations are independently specified.
  • Robert Almgren and Neil Chriss — Optimal Execution of Portfolio Transactions (December 2000 manuscript), sections1–2.1 — Primary research context for balancing expected execution cost and cost variance, with separate persistent and temporary effects. Our finite binary-shock model, within-block price integral, integer capacities and authorized size grid are original and have their own explicit convention.
